utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Unlike Mr. Koumjian, I know who my case manager is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good morning to you, too. So shall we call in the witness? He doesn't enjoy any protective measures, if I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he doesn't. Just before he comes in, can I just make certain that Your Honours understand? I'm calling him from scratch because the only time he's testified in Tadic, and the emphasis of the case was completely different there. And although I will try not to cover in too much detail matters that we already dealt with, which I know Your Honours have read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's your witness, I won't interfere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The other thing is I don't know Your Honours were given or we have a war diary of the 1st Krajina Corps. Mr. Ackerman, I think, mentioned it. It's going to be used very briefly by us. It's huge. The translation runs to 275 pages, mainly because each section has been photocopied to look like a diary. So there is one copy of the whole thing available. But what I was proposing to do was to only direct his attention to certain parts, put those parts up on to the ELMO at this stage, and then thereafter, give all of Your Honours copies of the pages that have been used so there will be one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be better, Ms. Korner, because if we only need to refer to a very small part of his diary, then there is no sense in bringing it up and taking it down every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's not his diary. No. "Diary" is not the right word, it's his work notebook. That work notebook, Your Honours will virtually need the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we talking of the document which starts with the ERN number 01104642?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes -- no, that is his diary. It's his -- I've called it a diary. I'm informed that's wrong. It's his official notebook. But in addition to that, underneath you'll see listed war diary of the 1st Krajina Corps on the list of exhibits, if Your Honours have that, list of documents to be used. It's on top of the bundle that Your Honours were given, unless Your Honour's secretary has reorganised it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably she has.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, I will check as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just -- and then if Mr. Ackerman uses any other further pages, whatever he uses we will then put a bundle together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The usher has gone to -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Selak. And welcome to this Tribunal, where you are about to start giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that this is not the first time that you have given evidence before this Tribunal and that you are familiar with the procedure, so I won't take -- waste any time in introductions. Please take the text of the solemn declaration that is being handed to you, read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that during the course of your testimony, you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. You may sit down. The procedure is as it was in the Tadic case. You will first be asked a series of questions which are expected to last for something like two days by Ms. Korner who is the lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case. She will then be followed by Mr. Ackerman who is the lead counsel for the accused, Radoslav Brdjanin. Thank you. Ms. Korner, he's yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, could you give us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Osman Selak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you born on the 20th of May of 1935?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you were born in Visegrad, which is in the eastern part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Could the volume be turned up a little bit, please? I'm having difficulty hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, please. Could we have a test transmission so that we can confirm that the volume now, volume level, is the right one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, can you -- first of all, are we sure that it is -- it must be because he was understanding what I was saying before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it to your satisfaction now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think it's right that you are a Bosniak by nationality?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And until September -- until June of 1992, were you a serving officer in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Until the 10th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to deal with your leaving the JNA or by then as it had become in Bosnia -- the VRS, but I think it's right that you applied to leave at the end of May. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The 19th of May, in 1992, I submitted my request for retirement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As you've told us on the 10th of July, you handed over your responsibilities to another officer and were you actually, however, formally granted your request for -- to retire in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's better if the microphone goes closer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. The usher will look into that. I notice that one of the microphones is not switched on. It's switched on now. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you left the military in 1992, had you achieved the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, before I deal with your specialisation and matters pertaining to the operation of the military, can I just deal with statements and testimony that you have given before for the purposes of the record? I think that you testified in June of 1996 in the trial of the Prosecutor against Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Having earlier made a statement about the events about which you testified over a period of months between 1995 and January of 1996?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When I say "a period of months," there were a number of separate days during that period. Did you then make a further statement in -- it was signed in July of 2000 but you had been interviewed or seen and looked at documents in January of that year?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you make a further statement in -- sorry -- March of 2001?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, were you seen on a completely different matter, really, by people unconnected, by investigators unconnected with this trial in respect of Manjaca, to do with the association of camp detainees?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And that -- I'm sorry I should give the date of that one -- was in August of 2001. Now, Colonel Selak, did you serve in what was then the major part of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, from 1955 until 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was your specialisation within the military the area of logistics?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, the technical services.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, just very briefly, can you explain to the Trial Chamber what that particular department would deal with.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The logistics service was in charge of providing the logistics, including all materiel, weapons, maintenance and also all the supplies relating to construction, technical and other supplies in the zone or in the area of its responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, dealing very briefly with your duties really with the -- what was called the Banja Luka Corps, after various other assignments during the course of your career, in 1977, were you assigned to the 993rd technical base in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In 1993, no. In 1977 -- in 1977, I was the deputy commander of the technical base in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It must have been a problem with interpretation, Ms. Korner, but we have sorted it out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you then spend the remainder of your service actually in the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. My whole term of duty, I spent in Banja Luka, from the academy until the time that I retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And can you just tell us what year were you promoted to the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did your area of responsibility cover a very large area indeed, in respect of logistics?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. The region of all the units in the region of Bosanska Krajina, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as far as the maintenance of tanks was concerned, this area was even broader.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to you have a look, please, at a map that was prepared for the purposes of the Tadic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that be perhaps put on the ELMO? It was originally marked as Exhibit 161 in Tadic trial. It looks like this, please, map number 1. All right. Perhaps rather than waste time, perhaps I can explain to the Registrar, I'm now going to go through all the maps that were in the -- and documents that were in the Tadic trial, of which you have all of them. But I will start so that we don't waste time using my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, Ms. Gustin perhaps could identify what would be the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, the exhibit number for this, Your Honour, will be P1548.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1548, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Selak, does that show your area of responsibility in respect of logistics prior to the 18th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So at this stage, you covered, as we can see, effectively from the bottom of the Bosnian Krajina and then going into Croatia at the top?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can see that Teslic and Doboj fell outside your area of responsibility. By what -- by which logistical unit would that be covered?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Doboj and Teslic were under the Sarajevo control or under the Tuzla corps area. I don't know the exact boundary between the Sarajevo and the Tuzla Corps but this is where the boundary was, somewhere to the right of Doboj, in between Teslic and Doboj. And this was until the 18th of May, 1992, that was the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you just tell us, we are going to look at a second map in a moment, can you tell us what was the significance of the date of the 18th of May?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The 18th of May, that day, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was officially declared. After that, the area was also shifted, the Banja Luka Corps zone was expanded to the east of Banja Luka, north-east of Banja Luka, in Bosnia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. You can take -- that can be taken away and can you be shown, then, the second map marked "map 2"? All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will become, then, Exhibit 1549.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other one we had, Ms. Korner, but this one we have not been given.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you have. I can assure Your Honour you have.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's not in the bundle of the documents. I only have map 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We only have map 1, actually, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's on the ELMO. We'll check it at the break. Maybe it's just me, Your Honour, but every time I appear in front of Your Honours there always seems to be a problem with the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, okay. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know it's there, Your Honour. And it's also in the registry's bundle. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In any event, Colonel, we can see it's on the ELMO now, does that --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that show the alteration in the area of responsibility, as far as you were concerned, with logistics?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we can see that one of the differences is that it now includes Teslic and Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Teslic, Doboj, Modrica, north-east towards Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Even on the 18th of May, it still included, did it, areas within the -- what was by then the declared Republic of Croatia, independent Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. It remained as part of the logistics service, the units -- our service maintained all the logistics for the units that were in the area of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So on the 18th of May, there were still units, were there, remaining in the area of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, it's not shown on that map, but we are going to hear evidence about the forward command post at Stari Gradiska. Can you just indicate, just looking at that, can you show the Court where Stara Gradiska was just roughly?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Stara Gradiska is over the Sava River, Bosanska Gradiska is to the right and Stara Gradiska is immediately next to Nova Gradiska. There was a famous correctional facility where those who were sentenced were serving their sentences, and this was changed into the command post of the 1st Krajina Corps from the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes. Thank you. Yes, that can be taken off the ELMO now. Now, I want to come back, then, and go into a little bit more detail about how the logistical supply --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know what Your Honours have now been handed, but I don't think it's got anything to do with what we are doing at the moment. Right. Your Honour, can I just explain, I don't know why they were handed to you now but they are just additional exhibits. They've got nothing to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They are simply extra exhibits that were disclosed and not even put in I thought. If Your Honours just put those aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you, please, about next, how the, as it were, command structure worked, in terms of logistics, the hierarchy. And I think the best thing is if you could please be shown now what was marked in the Tadic trial Exhibit 168, which looks like that. All right. Let's put my copy up again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, may that then be marked -- we had two spare exhibit numbers so we went back to them, but this will be 1561. I've just read it. It's in English but perhaps if you can just explain to us how the hierarchy in distribution of logistics worked, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The chain of command functioned from the general staff of the Yugoslav People's Army in the -- in Belgrade, of the Yugoslav People's Army in Belgrade. So it went from the general staff to the army commands to the commands of the bases, from the base commands to the corps commands, from the corps commands to the brigades, from the brigades to the battalions, and from the battalions to the companies. Those were orders. Whereas requests were put forth the other way around, companies, brigades, corps, base commands, army commands and then to the general staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So as you say, it was a two-way flow, either orders would come from the top or requests would be made through the various levels from the bottom?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, we can see, if we look at the left of this diagram, we can see national contracts, contracted suppliers and local contracts. Can you explain to us what is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. The complete logistics of the Yugoslav People's Army went through the economy of Yugoslavia. All the facilities and capacities of the economy of Yugoslavia were used, contracts were made with companies, manufacturer organisations, overhauling organisations, and all others. These were multi-year contracts throughout the territory of Yugoslavia. This went through the bases. The bases and the federal secretariat for national defence and army commands made these contracts; corps and individual units did not make individual contracts. They simply put forth their requests for logistical supply to the bases and then the bases organised everything else. As for what we did not have, we sent requests to army commands and to the general staff. This particularly has to do with ammunition, weapons, tanks, and other lethal weapons that the economy of Yugoslavia did not manufacture. This required import from other countries. Actually, some of it was provided for from the manufacturer of Yugoslavia itself because the former Yugoslavia had a rather powerful military industry. We even made tanks, APCs, aircraft, guns, et cetera but some was imported from other countries. However, imports went through the general staff. It is only the general staff that could sign contracts for those needs that we could not meet by ourselves within Yugoslavia. Then agreements had to be made with other states in order to have this kind of equipment provided. I personally in Banja Luka, my base command, signed contracts with companies in Krajina, that is to say for meeting the needs for the units of -- within the area of responsibility of the base command in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just amplify some of that? What sort of supplies were provided by these companies with whom the army had contracts?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I'll make an effort to speak slower. I'm talking about the base in Banja Luka, but the same situation was in other bases. We used mostly food supplies, service organisations, then construction material was provided -- were provided from construction companies. Medical services. As for what the army did not have and for the emergency medical services that the army could not provide, and then there were also transportation agreements that were signed. Companies wanted to cooperate with the army as much as possible because the army paid everything promptly. We even gave lines of credit to certain companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did the, as it were, the local companies ever provide ammunition or anything like that, or was that all dealt with at the top level?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: These local companies did not supply ammunition directly to units. There were only a few companies in the territory of Yugoslavia that manufactured ammunition and that ammunition went to warehouses of logistics bases and logistics bases, upon request from corps and other units, sent these supplies not directly to the corps but to the brigades because corps did not have their own warehouses, their own depots, so it was the brigades that received these supplies directly. The base sent its own transport vehicles to the company concerned, and then on the basis of the request put forth by the units, then we would supply those units with the material requested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, these supplies that you obtained, either ammunition and weaponry from above or the ones you organised yourself locally, to whom were they distributed? In other words, I'm sorry, can I tighten that question slightly. Was it purely to the corps itself, the regular army, or to the members of the TO?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. This was also sent to the members of the Territorial Defence, but the logistics bases did not provide for the Territorial Defence, at least not in peace time. The Territorial Defence was at the level of the republics. That was the -- its maximum level. And it is the republics that made contracts with companies that manufactured ammunition, or rather, if the army had a surplus, then they sent requests to the army and then the army would supply them with this for training these units when they had training for targeting, shooting, et cetera, but then this was basically dealt with at republican level. When the system functioned, then they sent requests to the bases and then we properly informed the command of the army about that. So this was resolved by telephone and then there was proper administration through documents as well, depending on the needs of the Territorial Defence. Also, we sent to them our surplus weapons, surplus equipment, too, the one that was not required by the Yugoslav People's Army. Usually these were dated weapons, and as for new types of weapons, only those that were truly a surplus in the army. So the Territorial Defence units had rather dated equipment and weapons, and they kept that in their own depots and warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, finally, before we look at some other aspect of military life, for supplies to be issued to members of the corps within your area of responsibility, did you have to authorise that distribution? Or your -- obviously your subordinate officers if you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Requests for logistics, in order to meet the needs of the corps, came directly to the base command. Mail also came to me. And then I distributed it to the heads of the various services, the technical service, the construction service, et cetera, and they directly resolved this with the heads of services of the corps. The head of service of a corps would say which brigade would have to be provided with ammunition or any other material. So it is the heads of services actually who resolved these matters directly because it is within their line of work and they are the professionals that know how to do that properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand the heads of services did it, but did you have to authorise the actual -- if there was a large-scale request, for example for more uniforms, would that be something that you would have to authorise?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The heads of service knew quite clearly how much equipment was needed by each and every unit. Every unit depended -- had the right to 5 per cent more equipment in terms of what they actually had so that they could intervene on their own if they needed extra equipment, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: But if there were some abnormal requests, then I would be informed about that and then I would react. Otherwise, this was a system that had been operated very -- had been operating very well because the army command and our command functioned properly and there were telephone conversations every day and all these matters were dealt with expeditiously on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm sure you heard that. Could you slow down slightly?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not -- the other thing is I think if you can try and keep your answers as short as possible -- and then if I want more information I'll ask for it. All right. Now I want to move, please, next, as a topic to the actual, as it were, makeup of the -- what was then the 5th Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. Could you now be shown, please, what was Exhibit 169 in Tadic. It's the diagram. And that will become Exhibit P1562. In fact, it shows the offices relating to the support of the logistics system, as it were.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again this is before the 18th of May, 1992. What you can see is the office -- the names of the officers in charge of the various levels that you indicated in that earlier diagram. Colonel General Adzic at that stage was chief of the general staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Chief of the general staff of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then was his assistant for logistics effectively the gentleman we can see there Lieutenant Colonel General --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Vladan Sljivic. He was a mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as these are all names that are going to reoccur and have already been mentioned in this case, we can see going across the page, can we, there was Major General Djukic, who was head of technical administration?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Djordje Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then moving down, Colonel General Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Commander of the 2nd army district in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then under him, Major General Milicevic. And then coming --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: He was assistants commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Coming down we see the 5th Corps and what's shown there is General Talic and Colonel Tepsic. But in 1991, who was the commander of the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It was General Nikola Uzelac, General Lieutenant Colonel Nikola Uzelac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was he replaced by another general before Talic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. On the 28th of December, 1991, it was General Vukovic who was appointed commander of the 5th Corps. Before that, he was corps commander in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think he was then killed and was replaced by General Talic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. when?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. General Vukovic was transferred to Nis, to the position of corps commander and he was killed in a helicopter accident when he flew to Pristina, so then when General Vukovic left in the month of March and he went to Nis it was then that General Talic was appointed commander of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then we can see that his assistant commander for logistics was Colonel Tepsic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Vaso Tepsic, Colonel Vaso Tepsic, assistant commander for logistics until he was killed in 1992 in a traffic accident. He held that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then if we go to looking at the right side, we see as it were, your direct unit, chain of command. Yourself?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Cendic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Rade Cendic. He was a colonel and he was also deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then we see the other officers whose names we'll see in some of the documents we are going to look at. But I wanted to move to a slightly different topic based on this. Looking at these officers whose names are mentioned here, what was the nationality, the ethnicity, of these officers, if we can just deal, going through the top, Colonel General Adzic first?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: General Adzic is a Serb from Herzegovina, from Gacko.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't bother telling us where they come from. It may become relevant later but just the ethnicity. The next gentleman?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Vladin Sljivic, Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Djukic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Brkic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Milicevic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Talic, we know. Tepsic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Yourself, a Bosniak. Then below you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Camic is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Camic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Mujo Camic is a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Vukovic is also a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that after we've looked at the second document in relation to this logistic support. Could you look, please, at what was marked Exhibit 170, which will become P1563. Thank you. This shows the logistical support after the change of the 18th of May, 1992, by which time, of course, there was a Serbian Republic of Herzegovina. And we can see the change in the general staff that at this stage General Panic was chief of the general staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stevilovic remains the same?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Djukic, the head of technical administration, becomes, in fact, Colonel Brkic -- I'm sorry, he remains the same?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, no. Djukic became assistant for logistics in the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. He was subordinated to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I'm sorry. It's Colonel Brkic remains in the same position as he was prior to the 18th of May?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Brkic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, my error. We can see there that Colonel General Mladic was the commander, then Djukic, Talic, and Tepsic remain the same. And the change in your chain of command, directly below you, there is a change from Lieutenant Colonel Camic to Major Milan Spiric?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, head of the technical service, Camic, Mujo, had to go to Belgrade. Major Milan Spiric came, a Serb from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to why it was that Lieutenant Colonel Camic had to go to Belgrade in May, but can I return, then, thank you, please, to the question of the ethnicity of the officers in the JNA before it transformed -- before part of it transformed itself into the VRS? By and large, and we can put the diagram away now, thank you, by and large, before -- and I want to concentrate on the period before the conflict started, effectively in April, 1992 -- what was the ethnicity of the officers in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The officers, in terms of ethnicity, came from all the republics or rather from all the peoples of Yugoslavia. Slovenes, Croats, Bosniaks, Serbs, Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you pointed out that all the officers save for yourself and your junior officer that we saw on that diagram were Serbs, of Serb nationality?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How was what we saw on that diagram reflected overall in the officer corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: As for the information that I have myself, yes, that is precisely the ratio that existed, about 90.5 per cent were Serbs and Montenegrins, that is to say the officers of the Yugoslav People's Army. And the others Slovenes, Croats, Macedonians, Bosniaks and others, only accounted for 9.5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The army itself, we've heard about the Territorial Defence aspect, but roughly what sort of size was the standing army, the regular army, leaving out all, Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: You mean the entire territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, actually, all I think for these purposes all I need to know is for the purposes of the 5th Corps of the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In peace time, as for the area of responsibility of the 5th Corps, there was the military academy for tank operators and then the reserve officer school for tank operators and the centre for drivers for combat vehicles, for the entire territory of Yugoslavia. That was also stationed in Banja Luka, and there were 6 to 7.000 -- 6.000 to 7.000 persons there in peace time, but as for officers, there were 6 to 700.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters correct 900 to 1.000 there.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: But as I already mention there were far more military personnel. There were that many officers because there were so many important institutions there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, very quickly, can we just look at the other diagrams which relate to effectively the 5th Corps itself? First of all, before the 18th of May, Exhibit 171, which will be P1564, and there, can we see General Talic? You've explained the change in commanders. And then his staff, the assistant commander for morale, Colonel Vukelic, the chief of security, Colonel Stevilovic; the Chief of Staff, Kelecevic; Tepsic, we've seen; Colonel Vujnovic; and so on and so forth. And then under that, we can see the combat units. The 329th armoured Brigade commanded by Colonel Simic, where was that based?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: That was a very strong armoured brigade, an unit, which was situated in the Kozara barracks north-east of Banja Luka, about 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 343rd mechanised Brigade, Colonel Arsic, where was that based?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The next one is the mechanised brigade. Where was that, the 16th?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In the Kozara barracks in Banja Luka, where the armoured brigade was also located.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Derventa brigade, I think that's the next one, probably speaks for itself?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In Derventa, it had its own separate barracks in Derventa where it was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then finally the engineering regiment and what's the last one, commander of the --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The engineering regiment, the commander was Colonel Radivoj Tomanic, and that was in the Kozara barracks in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the last one?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The commander of the rocket brigade, Colonel Nikola Obradoff, also in the Kozara barracks in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And then, if you can look at the next diagram, which shows the senior -- the officers and senior officers after the 18th of May? P1565. And effectively, there is not a great deal of change in the officers there. I think --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Chief of the anti-aircraft defence, actually, he -- the person who came to perform that duty was Lieutenant Colonel Lazarevic, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right, that's the change?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The person who performed that job before he did was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And I think while we are on that diagram, we had better deal with Colonel Stevilovic. We've already heard evidence about that, it says 06, 92. I think that's an error, though. He was killed in July, so 07 of 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of intelligence service, Colonel Stevilovic, was killed in the month of July, the 2nd or the 3rd of July, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, and then finally, and those are the last two diagrams, and then I want to deal -- and one photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the last one is 1565. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you look at the two maps showing the locations of the units of the 5th Corps? Now, map 3, first of all, which will become P1566. Does that show where the various units were based?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. You can see here the responsibility of the corps until the 18th of May, 1992, and where its units were deployed Mrkonjic Grad, Jajce, Donji Vakuf, Glamoc that was covered by the 30th division in Prijedor was the 43rd Brigade and then Banja Luka was the armoured.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak slower?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, could you slow down slightly?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In Banja Luka was the armoured brigade, the rocket brigade, the engineering regiment, the 16th Brigade, and some of my logistics unit, the maintenance, the tank maintenance capacities, the 343rd Brigade was in Prijedor. Mrkonjic, Jajce, Donji Vakuf, and Glamoc was covered by the 30th Partisan division way was commanded by Colonel Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. At this stage, did that come under, the 30th Partisan division, the authority of the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And now can we look, please, then, at the map 4 showing the locations after the 18th of May, 1992? P1567. And effectively it echoes, I think, what we saw on your logistics map, is that right, in that we now have unit --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Teslic and Doboj?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, and Modrica, Derventa, Modrica, Doboj, Teslic, an operative group was formed in Doboj which covered -- which covered Modrica and Teslic. The operative group was under the command of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just to deal with that, I think the area of responsibility of the 5th, which then became the 1st corps, 1st Krajina Corps, changed somewhat over the period of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, finally, on documents or pictures for the moment, uniforms. The Court has heard descriptions of the uniforms worn by the military. How many types of uniforms were there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The peace-time uniform, we call it the olive-grey uniform for short, and that was the uniform for soldiers, and there was another olive grey uniform for officers, for mobilisation and exercises other uniforms were used, camouflage uniforms, which up until the time they are needed are held in the warehouses of the units or the bases. So each base was supposed to have the appropriate number of war uniforms in accordance with the number of soldiers, plus another extra 5 per cent for wear and tear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what would be described by the words "SMB"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Olive-grey colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's the, as it were, the peace-time uniform?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you finally please to have a look at a photograph of Colonel Popovic, which I know you've looked at before, which will become Exhibit P1568. Can we just put it on the ELMO? Yeah. It's here. Just put it on. It's only going to take a minute. I think you've identified that before as Colonel Popovic who ran Manjaca. All I want it know is this: What sort of uniform is he wearing?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: This is either a camouflage or a war uniform. A camouflage uniform could not be worn during peace time but only during war or upon call-up. The rank insignia for officers was on the left pocket. There were metal insignia, brass, yellow brass insignia. The reason for that was so that a sniper would not see the rank insignia on the shoulders. So instead of wearing the rank insignia on the shoulder, for security reasons, for the safety of the people, the insignia was worn on the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We can take that away now. Did I give that an exhibit number? I did. Yes. 1568. Now, I want to move, Colonel Selak, please, to elicit from you a brief description, if I may, of the reporting structures which existed in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Will Your Honour forgive me a minute while I just find -- if Your Honour wants, it's the statement of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked to give detailed information about it, but I wonder, if I may, I want just to try and summarise this. In peace time, first of all, what would be the reporting done to the commander of the 5th Corps? First of all, that's a rather loose question so I'll rephrase Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that. Would he receive reports, first of all?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Twice a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From whom would he receive those reports?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The corps command had a team on duty, an officer on duty, who collected information from the units and from the different garrisons, and then he would convey all these reports, all this information, to the corps commander or whoever was performing his job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How often were the units, garrisons or the brigades, obliged to present their reports to the, as it were, the officer on duty?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Regular reports were sent in the morning, the situation at 7.00 a.m. By 8.00 a.m., it had to be submitted reporting on the situation up to 7.00 a.m. Also, the second report had to be submitted by 8.00 p.m., with the situation as of 7.00 p.m. So these were regular reports. Emergency reports, if something happened, had to be sent to the officer on duty, and he was the one who decided whether the corps commander had to be informed or whether the staff at the corps was able to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just give us one example of what would require an emergency report.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Any emergency situation, a person being injured, a traffic accident, any political problem, in any unit, was something that the corps commander had to be informed about immediately, as well as of the steps that were taken in order to resolve the problem. After that, he had to inform, depending on the gravity of the problem, his superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did those twice-daily reporting requirements, plus the emergency report that might be required, was there a change in that, if there was a time of war?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Reporting was continued with the same method and at the same time. However, at the corps command, there was a management team that was formed, an operative team, that could command the units on behalf of the commander if the commander happened to be away from the command. So that management team knew the tasks of all the units as set by the commander. And if the commander went away, he could perhaps convey to them some additional tasks, which then they would convey to the units, and the units had to carry out those tasks because the management team was speaking on behalf of the commander. So this was a valid command to the subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this management team, operative team -- I'm sorry perhaps we ought to have the diagram of the officers in the 5th Corps command. Could you be shown, please, again, Exhibit 172, whatever that was, 15 -- Exhibit P1565? The old Tadic Exhibit 172. If the commander -- let's call it for the purposes of this question, Talic, was elsewhere, who would form part of this management team?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: If the corps commander was not at the command post, he had a deputy, the Chief of Staff, and in this case was Colonel Bosko Kelecevic. However, the management team comprised of officers, colonels, the heads of services of the corps command, they were the heads of the teams. And from each branch, there was another officer every day in the management team so that he was -- the chief of communications or the chief of intelligence would each provide an officer. So they were able to expertly respond to all the problems that cropped up in the units during the day, and then the officer on duty of the management team would issue orders to the unit. However, once the corps commander came back to the command, the management team or the chief of the team had to inform the commander of all the changes and inform him about all the orders issued to the units so that the commander would know what had happened in his absence and that he could then continue with his command duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, did the system of reporting change after the 18th of May, and the formation of the VRS, or essentially did it remain as it was in the JNA days?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The system that functioned during the JNA was strengthened in manpower and communications and it continued to function because there is no need to change something that functioned very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This was the reporting that came from the subordinates of General Talic. To whom did General Talic himself report?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The management team would gather information from the subordinated units, and it was also obliged twice a day to inform the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in Pale, as well as of emergency situations, if they occurred, as they happened they would have the duty to inform the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and General Mladic about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, supposing it was decided that a military action of some kind had to be launched, let us take in a time of war -- for example, let us take the attack that we all know happened, leaving aside how, what exactly, that took place on the town of Kozarac. How would that have to be set out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The corps commander issued orders to all commanders of units or brigades in the territory covered by those brigades. The military, political, and security assessment was made in that area and the commander of the Prijedor Brigade, Colonel Arsic, knew exactly what his tasks were. They were given to him at the meeting with the commander in Banja Luka, attended by all the commanders, so that the commanders of other brigades knew what their duties and responsibilities were, as well as those of other commanders. This was in order to carry out coordinated action among the units. The dividing line was known between the brigades. But the responsibility for coordinated action was also there. So the -- each unit knew how far they could go to the left and to the right. The commander of the brigade in Prijedor knew what his tasks were. He didn't need additional orders; however, he prepared his units, at the sign, and the corps commander actually gave the sign to go ahead. But in extraordinary emergency situations, the commander of the brigade was the one who decided alone on the use of the unit. But he would inform the corps commander about that immediately, what he did, and the results that he achieved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I want to break this down so it may be appropriate to break at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 25-minute break. Is that fine with you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, I want to go over just a few of the things you said in your long answer. First of all, you said that the military, political and security assessment was made in that area. Who would make that assessment?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The assessment would be made by the corps command, together with the commanders of the subordinated units. Everyone from his own segment. The security organ presented their assessment. The morale organ presented their assessment. The traffic organ their assessment, and so on and so forth so everybody presented their own problems and their abilities to carry out the coming tasks. On that basis, the situation in the area was monitored in the municipalities, et cetera. So then these formations would also be taken into account when assessing units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, who would make the political assessment? Can you just explain very briefly, please, what you mean by the political assessment?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The assistant commander for morale and political questions, it was Colonel Vukelic specifically, had regular contacts with the political authorities in the territory. I'm talking about Banja Luka and the entire region. These political issues pertained to the following: What the political situation is like in the area concerned. For example, Banja Luka. He had to draw on the information provided by political authorities, political parties, the security organs, because everybody assessed the political situation as it affected their own line of work. On the basis of such assessments, decisions could be made on taking adequate measures for resolving current problems, adequate measures to resolve these problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you said that after the discussion, the orders would be issued to the person in charge, in this case Colonel Arsic, and then they would set out what he was to do. But in cases of unexpected, I think, I'm summarising because I haven't got the thing in front of me on the screen, he had the authority to carry out actions without orders, provided he reported it. Is that an accurate summary?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. He had full powers to carry out the task that he was assigned by his commander there and then on the basis of those assessments. He had the power and the responsibility to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the original orders you said would come from the corps commander. For an operation such as Kozarac, would he have to seek authority from his superiors, that is to say the main staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The corps commander had already been given an assignment from his superior, that is to say General Mladic, and the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. The corps commander knew what his tasks were, and when returning from reporting to Pale or from the command post of the main staff, he would call the commanders of the units, he would familiarise them with the task involved and then convey to them his orders in relation to carrying out that particular task. After that, the commanders of units would, on the basis of the task they had, elaborated in -- elaborate in detail the way in which the task would be carried out specifically, according to separate units, and what the responsibility of each and every subordinate unit commander would be in terms of the implementation of that particular task. The timing would be specified, the time when the task would be carried out and also reporting on each and every stage of the implementation of the task involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This is the next question I want to deal with. How strict was the requirement that the stages of the operation should be reported, the stage of implementation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: This is a legal requirement too. This is regulated by legislation, that is to say the functioning of military organisations, that subordinates have to report regularly to their superiors on each and every stage of task implementation. Also, on possible problems that they may encounter, and if they need additional information too. Then the commander, the superior commander, would give them additional orders if they would encounter problems, or rather if they would be in a dilemma as to how to resolve these problems. And then such a person would have to consult his commander in order to see how the task would actually be carried out. Commanders of units or rather the corps commander and his subordinates have the duty to tour these units on a daily basis and to have personal insight, and to render necessary assistance to their subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, supposing, during the course of a military operation, part of the forces under the command of the, in this case, Colonel Arsic, had got out of hand and behaved improperly in some form or another, putting it neutrally. Is that something that Colonel Arsic would be obliged to report to his superiors?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: If somebody would disobey or act contrary to the instructions received, the commander of the brigade - I'm now talking about Colonel Arsic specifically - could caution such a person, replace such a person, appoint another officer, but at the same time, he would have to report to the corps commander about the measures taken, and the reasons why he acted the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if the -- it was reported to the corps commander, in this case, General Talic, that during the course of an operation, something again neutrally, had gone wrong, what would his obligation be in respect of reporting to his superiors?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The corps commander, after having found out about the problem registered at unit level would have to take action straight away. He would send the person in charge to the unit concerned to see whether everything was carried out the way he had decided. At the same time, he reports to his own superior officer - namely, General Mladic or the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska - as to what measures he took.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, finally, on this aspect, if there was a major combat operation, would General Talic have to be given orders about that major operation by his superiors?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We may have to come back when we look at some of the documents to this issue of reporting, but I want to move now, please, to another matter connected with reporting. If a criminal offence occurred, either during civilian life or during a wartime operation or a military operation, what was the duty in respect of action taken, first of all by the officer directly concerned with the matter?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The officer in charge would have to take measures straight away in order to resolve the problem, or rather according to his own assessment, he could suspend or replace the officer who had violated the rules or had done something wrong. If the problem was a larger-scale one, then the military court would act.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who would be responsible for setting in train, starting up, the military court procedures?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The corps commander, and his organs would file charges with the military court, explaining the problem in detail, and then they would suggest to the Court for the Court to deal with the problems caused by the individual concerned, why this person had to be suspended from duty or replaced, why another person had to be appointed, another officer, instead of him, and then further proceedings are pursued by the Court itself, in accordance with its own jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can I move, then, to a slightly different topic? And that's this: I wanted to ask you about the relationship between the military and the political wings of government, and I want to deal first of all with it at the top level. What was the relationship between those -- the politicians at the republic level and the army at main staff level? In other words, who was -- who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The assembly of Republika Srpska or the assembly of the former Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yugoslavia was the top authority, the top political authority. The main staff or rather the general staff of the JNA or the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was subordinated to the Commander-in-Chief. When speaking of Republika Srpska, that is Mr. Karadzic. He was president of the republic. And the Commander-in-Chief of the Army of Republika Srpska. No other authorities had the powers to command and control the army. The hierarchy started from a soldier, all the way up to the Commander-in-Chief. That was the chain of responsibility. But apart from that, no political authorities could control the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Cooperation was inevitable and normal, but no one had the possibility or power to control.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'll come back to that in a moment, but what I want to understand is this: Did the army set its own goals or were those set for the army by the politicians, the political authorities?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The political authorities set the objectives and tasks that were to be carried out by the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How those tasks were achieved, was that a matter for the politicians as well or purely a matter for the military?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The military carried out their tasks, of course relying on the territory involved, that is to say on material and human resources. So there had to be cooperation between the sociopolitical organisations, the economy, and the army, at every point in time, all the way up to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to the point you've just made. The Chief of Staff, the Commander-in-Chief of the main staff, was subordinated to the commander -- to the President of the Republika Srpska, in this case, Mr. Karadzic. Before the declaration of Republika Srpska, under the old Yugoslavia, did the same apply in respect of the JNA, the main staff of the JNA, and the president of the old Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I mean I did not read their constitution but if you are talking about the SFRY, then there was a Presidency and the Presidency was the Supreme Commander, the Commander-in-Chief, of the armed forces. The general staff was subordinated to the Presidency of Yugoslavia. So there was an analogy with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The President of the republic was the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we move down the scale a little, as it were? What was the relationship -- and let's go to the bottom first -- between the municipalities and the army, the local representatives of the army there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The unit commander knew what his tasks were. It was normal that concerning part of the tasks he had, he should familiarise the political leaders in the territory where he lived. I'm talking about, say, Prijedor, and Banja Luka, the brigade commander had regular communications with the head of the municipality, just as I did in Mrkonjic, Jajce, and Donji Vakuf. Every day on a personal basis my commanders were there, they communicated with them, but I personally also communicated with them in order to see how we could help each other in carrying out our tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Slow down a little, please, Colonel Selak.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I keep forgetting myself. I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not your fault at all. I know it's difficult. You say you communicated with them, that is the head of the municipalities, in order to see how we could help each other in carrying out our tasks. Can you give us an example of something where you'd have communication.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Since I had subordinated units in Donji Vakuf, Jajce, Mrkonjic, and Banja Luka. In these three municipalities, Donji Vakuf, Jajce, and Mrkonjic, I went to see what the army could do in order to help the municipality and in which particular fields. In Donji Vakuf, for example, we built roads, repaired bridges. We used their own business sector for helping the unit, that is providing food, construction materials, et cetera, and this was in the interest of the municipalities involved too. So the heads of municipalities wanted the commanders of units to be coming immediately all the time, rather, and informing themselves about what was going on but also it was the managers of companies who had an interest involved. Then the secretariat for defence of the municipality involved would keep records of military conscripts, that were deployed in army units and in Territorial Defence units and that is why I and my subordinate commanders had to go to have personal insight as to these records, whether they were kept up to date, and whether people actually received accurate information in terms of mobilisation. That is to say where they had to report and at what time. So with regard to a great many issues, there were joint activities, normal activities, those that were to be expected, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in connection with this, I want you to look, please, at a document which I think demonstrates what you're talking about, about the cooperation. Could you have a look, please, at the document that's been marked 4.854?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a 5th Corps order dated the 14th of May, 1992. We found it. Thanks. And, Your Honour, that will then become P1569.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an order actually four days before the, as it were, change from the JNA to the VRS, and is the order -- is it signed on behalf of General Talic? Or by General Talic himself? No, I think it's on his behalf, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It was signed on his behalf. I saw this signature often, but right this moment, I cannot remember whose signature it is. But it is a familiar signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry, I don't think for these purposes it matters who signed it. Dated the 14th of May, the order, item 1, issues and problems, reinforcement, replenishment, I don't think we need trouble with, or 2. Item 3, "The corps command [assistant commander for civilian structures] shall resolve all issues relating to cooperation" --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Related to cooperation and coordination with civilian structures contained in requests submitted by the units upon receiving approval from the 2nd Military District command." And then item 4, "All requests for assistance, cooperation, and coordination of activities on the ground issued by civilian structures should be forwarded to the corps command," et cetera. The assistant commander for civilian structures on the 14th of May, was who? Was that Colonel Vujnovic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It was Colonel Gojko Vujnovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And does this -- this document, is that one of many documents that relate to the cooperation between the military and civilian structures?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just to note, in item 5, there is, "A verbal reporting shall be introduced because of combat activities," twice. So that was in addition, was it to the written reports that had to be sent in?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did the local brigade commanders actually report to the municipality leaders, the presidents of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Only regarding those matters that they felt the presidents of the municipalities should know something about that. Further than that, there was no need for them to be informed because it wasn't really reporting, it was just informing them. In the army, there is a system of reporting to the superiors, and informing on the level of equals, so there was no need to report but only to inform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could the civilian authorities, the municipality presidents, give instructions to the army at their level, again to brigade officers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Regular contacts were used and it was normal to expect that the aims were the same. The president of the municipality knew of the tasks and the aims of that unit, and naturally, they provided them with information that would be useful in the carrying out of the tasks of that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Supposing that they felt that something needed to be done, and let's jump ahead to the time of the conflict, that they felt that a particular area, village in their area, I should say, was some kind of a threat. Could they issue instructions to the local brigade to take military action?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The political bodies of the municipality, as part of their makeup, had armed police forces which could, and were obliged to, resolve minor problems, minor cases, and if they were not able to do that, the police organs, then the assistance of the army would be requested and in that case, the army would intervene and resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it was a request for assistance, rather than an order, to carry out the task?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. If the commander of the unit assessed that this was not outside of his area of responsibility or his jurisdiction. If it was within his jurisdiction, he would invest an effort to resolve that problem because it was something that touched upon him as well. It could create problems for him as well unless the problem was resolved, because the people from the municipality were part of his unit. So they were directly interested in resolving the problems in the municipality in a lawful and a proper manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we move to the -- actually the regional level? This was something I think that had not existed, the regional level of authority, until 1991-92, is that correct, in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Before the war, there were no regional associations, not at the level of Yugoslavia. There were republics and provinces, as well as the supreme authorities in Belgrade, the assembly, the federal government, and then as far as the army was concerned, the general staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Once this regional level of authority was established - and let's take it back to establishment of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in the autumn of 1991 - how did that level of authority interact with the corps in Banja Luka? In other words, who would it deal with at the corps? I'm sorry, I should actually go back. Were there dealings between the regional level of authority, and its leader, first of all Kupresanin replaced by Brdjanin when the Crisis Staff came in, and the corps in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. There were regular meetings, activities, accords were reached. The officers came to the Crisis Staff, and also from the Crisis Staff they went to certain areas where the units were, where they carried out certain activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we leave aside the Crisis Staff for a moment because again that's a separate topic. Before the establishment of the Crisis Staff in May of 1992, who dealt with the leader of the Autonomous Region of Krajina which up until then was Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Both the corps commander and his deputy for morale in the unit, that was Colonel Vukelic, contacted him. Or Colonel Gojko Vojinovic, who was appointed deputy commander for implementation of civilian authority within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the regional level authorities have any power, as the republic level did, to remove officers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could the regional level of authority give orders to the military?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the relationship, then, between the regional level of authority and the corps? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The regional organ of authority had information about the social, political and economic events in the zone, in the territory covered by that regional organ. At the same time, it was of interest for the army in that region, in that zone, to have life continue as normal within the law and the legal institutions and so on. So the army used the capacities of the territory which were there before that then, but they always reached agreements with the authorised institutions of the regional organs. They informed them about the tasks, the activities, and the use of the resources of the territory for the needs of the army, and the other way around. The army intervened in a certain area if there was a problem, so they carried out such tasks, the army intervened, but the regional organ was not. The political organ could not issue an order or an instruction to the army to carry out a certain task. The strategic aims were the same but the chain of command was well known.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what was the importance of there being a good relationship between, let's stick to the regional for a moment, the politicians in the region and the army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It was very important, because manning the army units was conducted from that area, the families of those people lived in that area, the economy worked both for the needs of the army, the army used those economic resources. So it was important for those relationships to be coordinated, harmonious, and to mutual benefit. That is why it was essential to reach agreements and that was something that occurred very frequently. And if any problem cropped up, it would be resolved jointly, either in the corps command or in the offices of the institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If a leader, a local leader, either at political or regional level, did not agree with the methods used by the army to carry out a goal that was agreed upon, what steps could he take to deal with that? What could he actually do?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The local organ, if they disagreed with any of the activities of the unit which was located in his area, was only able to request, but according to the hierarchy, so going up from him through the republican authorities to the government of Republika Srpska or even up to the president, Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. To request what? What could he request?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: They could request that the problem be resolved, the problem that this political institution felt should be resolved by the army and no agreement could be reached with the army, with the commander. The commander was obliged to inform the -- his superior commander about it. So if it was the commander of the brigade he should have informed the corps commander about that. And if the corps commander ordered him to do that in accordance with the agreement that they had reached with the sociopolitical organ, then they were obliged to carry out that task.
