It could also have come from the assembly, from President Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Karadzic, down to the corps through Mladic, and then be passed down to the brigade. So in reverse order, this order could have been issued to the brigade to do as they were supposed to. The local commander could have carried that out if he felt that that was in his jurisdiction. If not, he was obliged to refuse such a request.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, dealing specifically with the period between April 1992 and September 1992, were you ever aware of any disagreement between the army and the authorities, the regional authorities, in Banja Luka as to actions that were being taken by the army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I didn't hear about any such case, but quite the reverse. I only heard praise regarding this two-way informing and also there was gratitude to the army for the achieved successes in the achievement of their tasks. I haven't heard of any disputes, at least I cannot remember any right now. There was a problem in Teslic later, but I think that -- there was a problem in Teslic in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I want to deal as separate topics, your knowledge of and dealings with Talic and Brdjanin, but from your understanding of what was happening in that period of time, what was their relationship?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The relationship between General Talic and Mr. Brdjanin was always fair. They met often, exchanged information. I did not attend their joint meetings. Perhaps only on one occasion. But they were very regular, and we were satisfied with the relationship between the army and the staff headed by Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did there seem to be any divergence between the two of them in the political goals that the SDS and the VRS were seeking to achieve?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I could never reach such a conclusion, that there was any misunderstanding. Probably in the course of agreeing and coordinating their positions, perhaps there was some things that were not fully expressed, but in the media, in the public, and based on my contacts with people, I could never come to the conclusion that there was any divergence in any part or time frame while they were working together.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in general terms, as between the SDS and the VRS, leaving aside personalities at the moment, that is Brdjanin and Talic, did there appear that they wanted separate goals, separate ideas, in respect of a Serbian state?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The Party of Democratic Action, the SDS party, was in power. The president of the republic was the president of the SDS. So it was a common objective to achieve, to create, the state of Republika Srpska. And if that was a common goal, then they can only discuss how to reach that goal in the fastest and easiest possible way. There could only have been a divergence in the approach of how to achieve those goals, but the goals were common goals and there was no dilemma about that, nor was there any obstruction regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I now want to start dealing, please, with the events from the beginning of the war in Croatia. I'm going to be asking you to look at a number of documents but in particular, I want to establish a document that you yourself kept. Did you keep an official notebook during this period?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. There was an official, we used to call it the official notebook or the working notebook, log, and at the end, this log was certified with a stamp. It had its number and this document was an official document for court purposes. This is where all the tasks were noted down, who was given such tasks, and this was a document that was a valid document acceptable to a court. So it was an official document in the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you make notes at the time that you attended meetings or subsequently, or a mixture of both methods?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. Throughout my military career, carried those official notebooks and I would note down the moment that I was issued a task or if I issued a task, so I would note down in this official notebook the tasks that I was supposed to carry out. I personally wrote down in this notebook each official -- each officer was obliged to keep such a notebook for himself. The office -- or an officer could not enter the office of a superior officer without this notebook on him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you were at a meeting -- you say you've noted do you know if you were issued a task. If you were at a meeting and you were being addressed by the corps commander, would you write the notes of what was being said at the time or would you write it after the meeting had finished?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. I would write it as he was speaking, not only the commander but also when my subordinate was speaking I would be noting it down. So this helped me so that I could monitor myself while performing a task given to me, as well as monitor the task issued to my subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And I think you kept your work -- official notebook from the period -- when I say you kept, you retained in your possession from the period December 1991 until you left in June of 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. And I have it here in my briefcase.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, Colonel Selak has brought the original, in fact, it's been supplied to us sometime ago, the original is here, we've kept it safe for him. I don't want to make it an exhibit, because otherwise he won't be able to take it back. And I think the best thing is if he has the same photocopy that is part of our exhibit, and if necessary, he can go back to his original notebook. I'm afraid one of the problems as I discovered is that because, with respect to him, occasionally his writing is not the easiest to read for the translator, there are occasional errors that have turned up in the English translation. And I'm afraid it's because of his writing. So we may have to do some correcting in some of the editions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So, Mr. Selak, what's going to happen is this: You have your original with you, which you, of course --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- will make use of and consult in the course of your testimony. However, you're also going to be provided with the photocopy that we have of that original, and what I ask you is to ensure that when you are referred to a specific part of that journal or that logbook, what has been copied is exactly a replica of what you have. And if in the course of the interpretation you notice that there is some divergence, please point it out to us, because probably we will need your help absolutely in this area. The reason, it seems, is your handwriting. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm only wondering why he's being asked to use an inferior photocopy to his actual original. Why wouldn't he use his actual original?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that he has the photocopy just in case there have been markings added to the photocopy, et cetera. I just want to make sure that the photocopy is a faithful reproduction of the original, and I'm giving him that opportunity as he goes, he just has a glance. And if there is a divergence, he will let us know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only reason for suggesting the photocopy was this: That I know Your Honour is in the habit from time to time of looking at the original. His notebook is not paginated like the photocopies. That's the only reason. But I think if the colonel takes his notebook out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway we will try to render his life as easy as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we get to that, Your Honour, there are in fact, a couple of questions that relate to the period before. So it's all right, Mr. Usher, you needn't trouble with it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the war in Croatia broke out, as we know, in 1991, the middle of 1991. Was there any change in the way you were treated after the war with Croatia broke out, any particular example of a difference? Don't worry about your diary for a moment. I want to stick to 1991, before December.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's try and direct your mind to it because it's a rather too general question, I feel. Would you attend meetings with the corps commander on a regular basis, before September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did they begin normally at around 7.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there any change in those meetings, I'm sorry, in your attendance at those meetings after September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was that change?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In September, I was subordinated to the command of the 1st military district in Belgrade, just like General Uzelac. My base was subordinated to the command of the 1st military district in Belgrade. General Uzelac asked me to issue weapons to some Territorial Defence headquarters, municipal ones, which did not legally implement the call-up procedure of the TO units, which they were supposed to, under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause, sorry, Colonel Selak. That is something I want to ask you about, but at the moment, I was just asking you whether there was a change in the -- your attendance at meetings held after September, 1991. Was there a change in the time that you were asked to attend?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Before that, I regularly attended the meetings at the office of the corps commander at 7.00 a.m. in the morning. After that, I was invited to meetings at the corps command at 7.30. The corps commander had already covered some questions with his subordinates, which I did not hear and I did not know what had been discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am coming back to what you were telling us about the arming, but was there a change generally in the attitude to officers of Croatian or Bosniak nationality?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how -- what was the attitude? What was the change in attitude?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: There was distrust in relation to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that in relation to both Croatian and Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One can understand why Croatian, but why Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Because Bosniaks -- there was a referendum for the independence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's in 1992. Can we just stick to 1991.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In 1991, the units from the Banja Luka Corps went to the territory of the Republic of Croatia for armed operations, and the logistics base, my base in Banja Luka, covered all of those units regarding logistics, the ones that were on the border with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. I'll try to direct the witness to the question that you were asking of him. Ms. Korner referred you specifically to a particular point in time, and that's September of 1991, relatively speaking we are talking of the commencement of the war in Croatia. And you have stated, you have confirmed, upon a question -- answering a question that she put to you that the attitude inside the army towards Croatians and Bosniaks did change at this particular point in time. Ms. Korner told you, "I'm not surprised at all that there was a change this attitude directed towards Croats because obviously there was a war going on in Croatia. But she wants some kind of an elucidation from you why the attitude inside the army changed also with regard to Bosniaks when there was no conflict as yet in Bosnia, or a conflict which involved the Bosniaks. This is what you are being asked to explain. And after that, there will be further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosniaks did not respond to the mobilisation of wartime units that took part in the combat activities in Croatia. That is one of the reasons why there was this distrust, and why there were problems vis-a-vis the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What did you understand was the reason for your exclusion from the early part of these meetings with the corps commander? In other words, that you weren't told to come until 7.30 whereas the meeting actually started at 7.00?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I was a bit hurt by this personally, but it was my assessment that they discussed the tasks of the corps within its area of responsibility, and that I, as a Bosniak, should not hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you were starting to tell us about an incident involving a request by General Uzelac to supply arms to a unit, and I want to deal with arms, the supplying of arms, as a topic now. Can you -- you told us, I think, that you were requested to supply weapons to -- I'm afraid I've lost the part of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Some territorial forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you explain about this incident, please? And then I want you to look at some other aspects of this very topic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: General Uzelac, or rather the corps command asked me to issue weapons and other military equipment for Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where were those Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: This was Mrkonjic, Sipovo, Jajce. I think that one brigade was also at Kozara. I insisted that mobilisation be declared and that the legal requirements be met in terms of the issuing of these weapons. However, that was refused, and then I refused to carry out this order and that is how we clashed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now I think we need at this stage to ask you to explain what you meant. First of all, in order for a Territorial Defence unit to be issued with weapons, what had to happen?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was organised at the level of the republics. According to the law, in order for a unit to be mobilised and in order to have war equipment issued to it, from the warehouses, there had to be regular exercises in peace time. In a wartime situation and on the eve of a war, the declaration of mobilisation by the authority in charge had to be obtained. And that was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the legal requirement for issuing weapons and other equipment for the Territorial Defence unit concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So each -- if there was a general order for mobilisation, there still had to be a local order to mobilise the particular unit of the TO?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Every unit had to have its own. There is the Territorial Defence staff of a particular unit that would declare mobilisation and all of this is based on the superior authorities of the republic, and later on, since the TO took all the weapons from the JNA warehouses, then the federal authorities as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There, the three municipalities that you talked about, Mrkonjic, which I think it's Mrkonjic Grad, what was the majority -- I'm sorry, what was the majority of the inhabitants were of what nationality in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In Sipovo and Mrkonjic, there was a majority Serb population. In Jajce, there was a majority Bosniak or rather the Bosniak and the Serb populations were more or less equal. I'm not quite sure, but perhaps the Bosniaks had a 2 per cent majority in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at some documents now in relation to this arming but just generally speaking did a pattern emerge, as far as you were concerned, in respect of who was being given arms by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was being -- in general terms and we will look at specifics in a moment, who was being supplied with weapons?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: All mobilised units that were legally mobilised obtained weapons from their wartime warehouses. These were called the warehouses of the wartime reserves of the unit concerned. So it's not only weapons. It's ammunition and other military equipment, radio transmitters, vehicles, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just look at some documents, then, please? First of all, can you be given what was Exhibit 163 in Tadic, it's the document 00465065. And it will become P1570.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's written in the right-hand corner Exhibit 163. We will put the English up on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit whatever Your Honour just said, 1570. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this appears to be an order, does it, from somebody called Colonel Petrovic? You've been given? I'm sorry, what have you been given? Can I --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. I got General Kukanjac's commander of the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did can I --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, here it is, here it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. General Petrovic was whom?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Colonel -- Colonel Petrovic. Before the war, he was head of the technical service and the commander of the 5th military district in Zagreb. May I finish?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: When the command of the 5th military district withdrew from Zagreb via Bosnia to Sarajevo, Colonel Petrovic as a technical officer was deployed in the technical service of the command of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, does this order, it's an order to the logistics takes base command of the 5th Corps, was that your base command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I know about this document. I did not receive it. It was my assistant for logistics, Lieutenant Colonel Stamjenkovic [phoen] that received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This appears to be a request from ammunition and weaponry to reinforce the 3rd Territorial Defence detachment of the 10th Partisan division. Now, what was that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The 10th Partisan Division, whose commander was Colonel Radosevic covered the territory of western Bosnia. At that time, the corps command was not my superior; it was the army command in Sarajevo that was. All this ammunition was issued for this unit. There was no problem whatsoever with having it issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And that unit was of what nationality? Or the soldiers of that unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I think since this was already the month of February, that 99 per cent of them were Serbs. Perhaps even 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. But this, as far as you were concerned, was a perfectly proper order and proper supply of ammunition and weaponry?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. All the ammunition was issued and it can be seen in this document that there is a sign, a mark, on the right-hand side showing that this had been carried out. You can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I want to look at some further documents, please. Could you have next the document which is got the number 4.2160? Dated March -- it says March of 1992 on it. It's a report or conclusions rather, of the assessment of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I'm sorry, although in time -- may I stop that? Although in time it is the next document, I think because it covers a number of areas, I'd better deal with some of -- that we haven't touched on yet. Can I leave that in, I'm sorry. Can you now have, please, the document that was Exhibit 166 in Tadic? And it's a document dated the 24th of April, 1992, which will be P1571.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, this is a document I think you saw, indeed you dealt with it in Tadic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a document for the 24th of April, 1992, from the command of the 2nd military area, to -- who is it actually addressed to? Is it addressed to the federal secretariat for national defence?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. It was sent by the command of the 2nd Military District as very urgent to the federal secretariat for national defence, to the technical department thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we see that it states that, "From the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of BiH, we received a demand, top secret, for giving out material and technical assets to be used by the special militia unit from the centre for security service of Banja Luka." That's the CSB. And then we see a quite staggering list of requirements starting with helicopters to the -- at the top, and finishing off with medical equipment. Now, first of all, what was the special unit, special purpose militia unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: That is the special purpose militia unit for carrying out specific tasks, like mapping out the terrain, bringing people into custody. The special unit was not there in peace time. It was established only for wartime purposes. In addition to the regular police, they asked for this special purpose unit to carry out tasks that they were ordered to carry out by the political authorities. They were not under the jurisdiction of the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Was a request like this -- or in normal circumstances, would the military supply this sort of equipment to the police?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever in your - however many years of service - ever see such a request?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: This is the first request I have seen in my military career.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there any regulation that you're aware of that allowed the military to supply to a special police battalion or militia unit, this type of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: This was not the regular and legal way to arm the police, the special police unit. I see on page 4, where General Kukanjac, recalls the order of the chief of general staff of the armed forces of the SFRY and he refers to a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, there must be an error I think in the date there. It should be, it says we are reporting the demand in accordance with the order of the armed forces blah, blah, blah. It should, I think, be 1991, should it not, if we look --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, no problem whatsoever. This is April 1992. And this is orders by the chief of general staff, so no problem. Quite certainly, this is 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I issued equipment that the base had for meeting the needs of this police unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, can you look, please, at a document which I think may help us to understand what was happening? Could you look, please, at a document of the 31st of August, 1992? It was attachment 7 to the second statement, I think. And it's dated the 31st of August. Yes, July -- it's attached to the statement of July 2000. Thank you. I said second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1573, I think. 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, 72.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is headed: "1st Krajina Corps command, strictly confidential, 31st of August, 1992. Inventory of weapons issued to, Republika Srpska army, in response to your strictly confidential order of the 20th of August, we hereby attach the inventory of weapons and equipment issued to units and TO staffs; in other words, to structures outside the armed forces since the beginning of the activities, aimed at protecting Serbs from genocide in Croatia and the Serbian Republic. The weapons and equipment listed here were issued against a receipt and still figure on the ledgers of the 1st Krajina Corps units that actually issued the weapons. Please inform us of your opinion on this matter." Now, what do the words, "To structures outside the armed forces" mean?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Structures outside the armed forces are paramilitary units. Weapons were given to the Serb population at their homes. Except for the paramilitary formations, people received weapons at their homes as well during the night, in smaller towns and villages where there was a mixed population, ethnically speaking, houses were marked using black paint on walls showing that that would be a Serb house -- that that was a Serb house, rather. I personally saw that in Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that means outside the -- even the members of the Territorial Defence who had been mobilised to serve, does it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It says here, "Territorial Defence staffs of Municipalities."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the list. Before we look at the list, perhaps we should just -- this is going back to the time of the war in Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we now have a look, please, at the list that's attached. Is what is shown under the words, "We can see the STO, the territorial organisation," we see the various areas that it refers to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But may I say the following? Okucani is in Croatia. Kostajnica is in Croatia. Glina in Croatia. Sisak in Croatia. Dvor Na Uni in Croatia. Prnjavor is Bosnia-Herzegovina, Western Bosnia. Petrinja is in Croatia. Bosanska Krupa in Bosnia. Omarska in Bosnia. Sanski Most in Bosnia. Laktasi, Celinac, Bosanska Gradiska, Banja Luka. SUP, Banja Luka. The antisabotage unit, Banja Luka, and the Territorial Defence staff of Western Slavonia in Croatia. Bosanski Novi in Bosnia, Laktasi, and other beneficiaries. JNA, I don't know who this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You say that one of the things that this document shows is that the -- there was an issuing of weapons to paramilitaries, persons outside the mobilised units or the regular units. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I say that because the units of the corps and the Territorial Defence had been mobilised. They had their own weapons and all the equipment and ammunition. This was issued apart from that. I mentioned the staff of Western Slavonia. I know that they asked me for weapons for 2.500 men and official figures show that they had a personnel of 500 men. I did not issue these weapons because it was my assessment that this meant arming the people or paramilitary formations. As for this particular survey, all of this was issued. It was not the base that issued it. It was the corps units that did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we take, for example, the -- look at the ethnicity of some of these municipalities --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I see the time. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to draw your attention. We will have another break for 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the purposes of the record, I should say that Your Honours will see that I've been joined by Ms. Sutherland who finds matters more interesting here than in the Stakic case at present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, we were dealing with this particular document before the break, and I think we need to go through it a little carefully but first of all can we look at the ethnicities of some of these municipalities that are mentioned? Leaving aside the ones in Croatia, Prnjavor, was that a largely Serb-dominated municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. All except Sanski Most where it was about 50 per cent and 50 per cent of Serbs and Muslims, that ratio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about Prijedor, which I think also appears?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Prijedor also and Bosanska Gradiska, although the Serbs were in a majority in Bosanska Gradiska but it was a small percentage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you don't know the answer to this, say so because we can get the evidence from elsewhere. In respect of Prijedor, was the head of the TO, what ethnicity was the head of the TO? As I say, if you don't know the answer, say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about in Prijedor? Or did I say Prijedor? No, Sanski Most, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I don't know about Sanski Most either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the list is headed, "Weapons and equipment issued to the TO staffs and units of the 5th Corps." Let's just concentrate on the TO staffs. That seems to conflict to some extent with the wording of the original letter issued to units and TO staffs, in other words to structures outside the armed forces. Now, you've told us that this document reflects weapons being issued to individuals as opposed to lawfully to the TOs. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Because when it's issued to individuals, it's illegal, because a person has to get them from the authorised institution. I never issued weapons to an individual from the command. The procedure how a person is armed is well known, who signs for it, and whether this person has the right to carry a weapon also.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But why shouldn't this be a list of weapons and equipment issued to TO staff, leave aside again units, of the 5th Corps, as a legal matter? Why is it to individuals and not to the TO staffs themselves?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I know that retired officers and other persons received weapons from units of the corps, allegedly in order to guard different facilities and buildings and so on. I think that there was a document about that, but it's not here right now, where it is documented --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, don't worry, Colonel Selak, we will come back. I know the document you're referring to and we will be looking at that. But at the moment all I want to know is if we look at this list, which apparently was taken out of the ledgers of the 1st Krajina Corps, how are you able to say that this was -- looking at this list, this shows an unlawful distribution of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It is the 31st of August, 1992, here, and in the text, in the act itself, it says, "Since the beginning of the activities on the protection of Serbian people from genocide in Croatia and the Serb republic." Staffs of the TO do not need to have such a large number of weapons because their TO units have been mobilised and armed. So the staff only has a few -- a couple of people, four or five people, so I don't see the need for such a number of weapons and equipment to be given to the staffs. It must mean that they were issuing that outside of the TO units so that must have been to paramilitary units or giving it to the population in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. I think we are getting there. So this was issued to the staff - that's what it talks about - and not the TO unit itself?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in the light of what you know to be the number of a staff, if we look at the amount of weaponry that was handed out, for example if we look at Prnjavor, 121 rifles, if we go to Bosanska Krupa, 905?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Bosanska Krupa as well, 460 semi-automatic rifles and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: If I can tell you, the Okucani staff in Croatia issued 111 pistols - that was distributed to the population - and semi-automatic rifles, 900 of them. So this is illogical.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I follow you. Were you aware of any of this distribution going back, obviously, to 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As the person in charge of logistics for the 5th Corps, then becoming the 1st corps, should you have been aware that this had been going on?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It was normal for the corps to request the logistics base to request ammunition, weapons, and other equipment from the logistics unit, in order to resupply their units. So the base was the one who should have resupplied these units and not the corps. They were not subordinated to the corps because this is a territorial organisation. So they had to use other channels and use other ways to get the weapons and the equipment. That is why I have the figure for the corps in my documentation here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the number.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: That is precisely the number that is being indicated that the weapons and the equipment went to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the number, Colonel Selak, because the interpreter didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In my official note, notebook, I have put down the information that the corps numbered 100.000 people, which is not logical at all and it's not correct. And these -- this composition was reported as part of their number, and others as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think you've lost all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid because we have to go back to the figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say the official number of the corps that you've recorded was 100.000 people?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: If necessary, I will find it if my notebook, the place where I wrote that down, where there are 98.000 and a couple of hundred mentioned. That's the figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry about that, we are going to come to that because we are going to through your notebook logically. What we are trying to understand is what you're saying here in relation to the size of the corps and this document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. This document says that the corps also included these people as part of its number of men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what it actually says is that these were structures outside the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see, yes. Units of the -- yes, quite right, yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in fact, if I may butt in and perhaps you could direct -- address the point by putting a further question, is that, referring to the apparent conflict, that there is or divergence that there is between the letter, the memo, sent by General Talic, which is the first page of this exhibit, and the list, how can one come to possibly be able to distinguish which of these weapons and equipment went to TO staffs and which went to units of the 5th Corps? Because if there is no way of distinguishing between the two, we have a problem. Plus the penultimate column, other users, JNA, Yugoslav People's Army, perhaps he could address that and explain whether that is the units of the 5th Corps. I don't know. I mean it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is clear, Your Honour and Colonel Selak can explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, you heard the Judge's question. Of these columns we can see which are the units of the 5th Corps that are referred to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The other JNA users, I don't know which users he meant. The 5th corps or the 1st Krajina Corps, regarding that, it is quite known precisely how much weapons and how much supplies they should receive, plus 5 per cent over that. So the -- there are records of weapons in other places. So these weapons were actually given to these units. I don't know what they mean by "other users." Possibly they could only mean retired officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But it says, "Units of the 5th Corps." Are there any columns here that relate or could relate, given what you say that this was going to paramilitaries or individuals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can go direct, Ms. Korner, by referring him to particular columns. I can do that actually. If you go third, sixth, eighth, column where there is brigade and then TO, Bosanska Krupa, according to you, what does that mean? These weapons and equipment were delivered to who? Why do we have brigada here -- brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Brigades, units, that's one brigade. That is the brigade of the Bosanska Krupa TO which probably was called up mobilised later, and weapons were issued to that brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you go to the column that says -- I think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before that there is another one again but we want to make sure that it is just Territorial Defence units or whether it's something mixed or separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two columns before the Banja Luka one, Ms. Korner, OK, distribute, CTS, TOB, and then Banja Luka. And then there is another one, Banja Luka, which is two columns further on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't want to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you deal, first of all, with the column after Bosanska Gradiska and I think it's easier on the B/C/S than this one. What does that relate to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: That is the regional staff of the TO in Banja Luka. So this 63, 30, and 408 helmets were issued to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The next we get the SUP Banja Luka, which is the police, I think?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The secretariat for internal affairs, Banja Luka, that is the police, and that is why there are pistols , and also the sabotage detachment of Banja Luka, which is also not part of the 5th Corps. It was under the jurisdiction of the SUP. It received the rest of this equipment that -- and you can see that from this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So in fact, none of these columns other than "other users, JNA," could even remotely be units of the 5th Corps? They are all Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that represent, Your Honour? All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I want to make sure is that we do have the correct translation and the title. In other words, perhaps the witness can read the title and we can have a current, running translation of it, to make sure that it is "and the units of the 5th Corps." Do you understand me, Mr. Selak?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak could you just read out --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's clear to me. This is a report of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, stop, don't worry. Could you just read out. I'm sorry, you've misunderstood, Colonel Selak. Could you just read on the sheet containing the figures, could you read out so that we can get a translation, what it says.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Oh, to read the columns?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, just read the headnote.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. "Review of weapons and equipment issued to the staffs and units of the TO from the 5th Corps."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it makes it different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Here, it states that "Weapons and equipment was issued from the corps, from the corps reserves." They are talking about the equipment here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The translation that we have is exactly the opposite. It's to and not from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour is absolutely right. It's the way it's -- I'm afraid it's going to come up in another document which I picked up as well that we've had the translation shows it the opposite. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have cleared that up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is confirmed by the accompanying document. It confirms that it was -- the equipment and the weapons were issued from the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Had it been issued by the base, then it would state that it was issued by the base and there would be the numbers 99 there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we just summarise, if we can, Colonel Selak, before we put this document away what it actually shows? I think you've explained largely. First of all, it shows issuing from units, now that we've got it, from units of the 5th Corps, weapons to certain TO staff, or allegedly, I should say.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because it doesn't include -- this list doesn't include all the TO areas that came within the 5th or 1st Krajina Corps, does it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For example, Jajce came within, as we know, came within the area of responsibility and they didn't receive anything?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Jajce and Donji Vakuf and other municipalities did not receive anything. I don't know why. But perhaps the ethnic composition of the population also was a factor in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then the reason -- let's get this absolutely clear, the reason, as expressed in the letter, is that the -- the reason for issuing this was to protect activities aimed at protecting Serbs from genocide?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And because the size of the TO staffs was very small, in your view, this was a distribution of weapons illegally to individuals?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: But the corps is informing, based on the order of the main staff of Republika Srpska, it's reporting on what was issued, the staff asked for the same information from other corps. So this is a report based on an order issued by the main staff of Republika Srpska. So they had orders to issue this equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, yes. Thank you. Now, can we look, please, before we look at the major, the big document, at one further document in relation to this matter? Could you be shown, please, document 4.593? It's dated the 14th of March. It's a little earlier. Quite a lot earlier, actually. And it will be Exhibit P1573. Now, it's dated 14th of March, "Issue of weapons and ammunitions Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to the Banja Luka municipal Territorial Defence staff command, on the basis of genuine need for the issue of weapons and ammunitions and with the consent of the Banja Luka Territorial Defence staff, I hereby order that the following weapons shall be issued to the Territorial Defence unit in the village of Karanovac." And there we see the list. And then, "The commander of the TO opportunity staff Sergeant Mladjo Vranes shall receive the weapons, two combat sets of ammunition," and so on and so forth. And it's signed by your assistant commander for logistics. First, were you aware in March of 1992 that such an order had been given?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Should you have been made aware of this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: According to the rear support schedule, they should have contacted the base and not the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. First of all, I want to come on to that, but in the event that what was -- something extraordinary was happening like this, should your assistant commander have made you aware of this request?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: He should have consulted me and there would have been no problems, because I see here that the district staff of the TO of Banja Luka knew about it, even though the corps did not have these weapons, the base did, and the base would have issued them, but I -- I, however, didn't know anything about this. Nobody informed me about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this issuing of weapons to the unit in Karanovac, first of all what ethnicity was Karanovac, or what nationality were the inhabitants, I should say?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The local commune of Karanovac is up river from Vrbas, upstream of the River Vrbas, and it's 5 kilometres away from Banja Luka, and the majority of the population is Serb, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The request for weapons to be issued to the Territorial Defence unit, I think you've told us, but can you just say it again, to where should it have gone?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It should have gone through regular channels in accordance with the regulations of rear supply towards the base, from the municipal staff of Banja Luka, if I didn't have enough materiel I would have found a way to bring the material in from another base and to issue the weapons but this was a small platoon, about 30 soldiers, and Colonel Tepsic, the deputy assistant for logistics, did have the weapons and he issued an order that the weapons be issued from their reserves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just look at this? It says that, "He orders that Banja Luka Territorial Defence shall issue the following weapons." So he's giving an order apparently to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: He gave his approval. He approved it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In what circumstances would the Territorial Defence command be applying to the corps for these weapons?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I personally think that the Karanovac local commune, before the war, did not have a TO unit, that this was formed in March. The TO staff, the Banja Luka municipal TO staff, did not have enough weapons to arm this platoon, and this came back then to Colonel Tepsic, whether he could issue that from his supplies, and this seems logical to me, because Karanovac is at the entrance to Banja Luka, and with these people, they could control all exits and entries into Banja Luka because the main road to Jajce passed through this local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So what you're suggesting is that these people were being armed not to go to Croatia but to control the entry or control the roads?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And now finally, can we look at the major report for that month, which is 42160, the assessment of the situation? Now, this covers a number of topics and I think I'm going to come back to this report when we deal with the various topics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can it be produced at the moment as Exhibit P1574?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you turn, please, to the part of the report that is headed, it says, "Volunteer units in the 2nd Military District zones." And then there is a thing that says, "Personnel strength in corps zones." Actually I'm sorry, perhaps we ought to go back -- I think we ought to read this in context, paragraph 4, paramilitary organisations in BH. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, point 4 speaks about paramilitary organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Actually, on a party basis, the Muslims 60.000, the Croats around 35.000, and the Serbs around 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, first of all, I don't think we can deal with the figures so they are suggesting that there has been arming by the parties with the Croats and the Muslims on the face of it having armed a great deal many more people than the Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then it describes what it says are the main goals of the Croatian and Ustasha forces in the republic, and then goes on to deal with volunteer units. Now --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What, in your experience or understanding, is meant here by "volunteer units"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Volunteer units were established in all municipalities. This figure pertains to the volunteer units of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we look at that, it deals with the 2nd Military District which covered the 5th Krajina Corps --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The units are formed into companies, their total strength is 69.198. No volunteers are to be used to replenish the strength of the wartime units of the 2nd Military District, and only a small number belong to the Bosnia and Herzegovina Territorial Defence. Thus, volunteer units are outside the JNA and TO establishment."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very much goes along with that last document we saw. So these volunteer units are what? How would you describe them? You've said they were Serbs. What's the word you would use to describe these units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Volunteer units carried out tasks related to party affiliation. The SDS and the political institutions of the territories on which they were established. Actually, they were carrying out ethnic cleansing too, in the zones, but the army units did that to a lesser degree. This dirty work so to speak was carried out by these volunteer units, arrests, killings of people, maltreatment of people, et cetera, lootings and so on. So there it was an exodus, or rather an ethnic cleansing of the territory involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll come to that but I have no doubt you've heard of a -- of something called the Wolves of Vucjak. Are these what you would include or what you could consider are being described as volunteer units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: That is one of the best-known volunteer units that was well-trained, well-equipped, well-dressed and it was infamous for the atrocities and abominations it committed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then can we go down, please, to under D -- well, personnel strength and then we see, sorry, paragraph, subparagraph F, "The JNA has distributed 51.900 weapons to these volunteer units, 75 per cent, and the SDS, 17.298 weapons."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In order to get this information that the SDS had received 17.298 weapons, would there have had to have been contact between the SDS, whoever was responsible, and the army over this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: This is an evident example of everyday communication that the SDS got through the army all the necessary equipment, weapons, and the commander of the 2nd military district, General Kukanjac, precisely in this information gives the exact figures, gives figures as to how many weapons were issued for the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then under G, to date, "300 automatic rifles have been distributed to retired military officers in Sarajevo." And we don't need to bother about the rest of this. Were retired military officers entitled to receive weapons?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: They were not entitled to that. The army gave them this in order to guard their houses and their own lives, but it was done in an unauthorized manner, illegally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then can we look at some experiences? We see most of their armed Serbs do not want to leave their immediate area. They want to defend their village, neighbourhood, and military facilities. This refers to Serbs in areas where Muslims are in the majority. Second point made, "Some SDS leaders at all levels are seeking weapons from the JNA and the Ministry of National Defence through various channels in a fight for primacy which is causing division and dissatisfaction amongst the people." Colonel Selak, were political leaders entitled to be given weapons by the military, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: According to the law, they could not do this. There was no legal basis. However, the law was not observed. Weapons and ammunition were distributed to the Serb people. A considerable portion from -- a considerable portion of the weapons came from Serbia and Montenegro, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you don't know the answer to this, again, Colonel Selak, can you say so. Do you know whether any of, first, the regional leadership in Banja Luka was given weapons by the corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't know or they weren't, sorry?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Don't know. I don't know. I believe they were but I don't have any official information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's important that we just stick to what you know. Do you know whether any of the municipality leaders, like Radic and the rest, were given weapons? And again, if you don't know, say, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: But I did saw that automatic -- that retired officers in Banja Luka even had automatic rifles. If you want to, I can give you the names of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that unless Mr. Ackerman wants the names. Now, in this part of the -- this document, we see this: "Some SDS leaders advocate standing apart from the JNA and the creation of another army, which may affect the JNA adversely, particularly when it comes to troop replenishment of units." Now, we were dealing earlier with the relationship between the political and the military bodies. This paragraph seems to suggest that where there was a SDS leader who wished to stand apart from the JNA and the creation of another army, he could affect the military adversely, particularly when it comes to troop replenishments. Does that mean that the political leaders could have an effect in respect of replenishing the number of troops needed for units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. They had a significant effect in respect of replenishing the number of troops. That is why many did not respond to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did they achieve that effect? Was it their responsibility to ensure that there was a replenishment of the units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I am speaking about my own unit now. I had to ask for police intervention to have certain military conscripts arrested because they did not respond to mobilisation and to my own unit so I had to have the police bring them in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All that I'm asking -- I understand what you're saying but therefore the replenishment of the units, as it's put here, the bringing in of recruits, lay within the power of the politicians, the political leaders?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, perhaps that would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Colonel Selak, you deserve a break, but you need to return again tomorrow morning at 9.00 when we will continue with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wanted to raise something but I have forgotten all about it now. I meant to address you on something, Ms. Korner, but I have forgotten. So -- anyway, tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of January, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
